title: KV run-length compression: hot-run memory and spill behavior (WIP)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

This note captures an exploratory investigation into applying lightweight run-length compression (RLE-like signatures) to in-memory KV entries to reduce resident set fragmentation and NVMe spill pressure during long hot runs. The idea: many KV entries exposed by transformer inference (especially kv slices for early layers or attention heads with repeated vectors / padding) exhibit short repeated patterns or long contiguous equal-value words after quantization. If we can compress those on-residence with a very cheap encoding and decompress cheaply on re-use, we might reduce memory bandwidth and paging while preserving tail latency.

Top-level hypotheses:
1) Run-length compression of contiguous identical cache words will reduce effective resident memory and NVMe writeback volume for workloads with repeated padding-like segments and quantized zeros.
2) The CPU/GPU overhead of encode/decode will be negligible if we only compress when contiguous-run length > threshold (e.g., >= 4 words) and placement is on host-side meta pages (no full copy for small runs).
3) Compression reduces DMA burst sizes and evictions under bandwidth pressure, improving 95/99th latency under multiworkload mixes.

Why this is different from prior eviction/prefetch work:
- Prior notes focus on eviction heuristics, prefetch predictors, and TTL tuning. This doc tests a content-aware residency optimization that complements eviction: instead of choosing what to evict, we store objects in a denser representation to increase effective capacity.

Experiment design:
- Traces: two types
  - Synthetic app traces: short-token chat-like distribution (seqlen 128, mixture of 1–3 user turns) with dense quantized heads produced via quant-aware model sim.
  - Production sampler: 24-hour slice from production 2024-11; extracted KV write patterns and word-level histograms (obfuscated).
- Runtime build: experimental branch rle-compact-v1 on PR 978. RLE is applied to host-side serialized KV pages before residency promotion. Minimal metadata (run length, value) appended to page header. Decompression done in the hotpath on cache hit if compressed flag set.
- Hardware: p4d-like node (8xA100 equivalent) with 1TB host RAM, NVMe-backed local SSD; synthetic runs on dev machines (A10g), production-sampled runs on staging cluster.
- Metrics collected:
  - resident memory (bytes), resident entries count, average entry size (post-comp), NVMe writeback volume and IOPS, host->GPU DMA bytes, per-request p95/p99 latency, CPU cycles in encode/decode, eviction rate (entries/sec), and KV hit ratio.
- Profiling hooks:
  - perf+flamegraphs for host encode/decode code paths
  - nvprof to measure GPU-side stalls linked to DMA throughput
  - eBPF capture for NVMe writeback bursts and kernel queue latency

Threshold tuning:
- Compression only when contiguous identical word runs >= T, with T in {2,4,8}. Also only when entry size >= S where S in {64B, 256B, 1KB}. We tested combinations where compressibility gain > 20% to avoid churn.

Key results (aggregated) — synthetic traces:
- Effective resident bytes reduced by 12–28% depending on T/S. Best tradeoff at T=4, S=256B => 18% resident reduction.
- NVMe writeback (by volume) reduced 15–33% in runs where synthetic trace had many padding-like entries.
- p95 latency improved up to 9% in multiworkload saturation tests; p99 improved up to 5% in these synthetic tests.
- CPU overhead: encode cost averaged 0.9% of request cycles when using background encode (post-promote) and synchronous decode cost added ~120–180ns per compressed hit (measured on staging dev nodes).
- Eviction rate decreased by 8–20% because denser representations delayed spill thresholds.

Key results — production-sampled traces:
- Resident reduction median ~7% (lower than synthetic) — because production traces have fewer long contiguous equal words after quantization. However tail cases where a large batch of similar-length sequences occurred showed up to 25% reduction locally.
- NVMe writeback reduction median ~9%. Bulk writebacks reduced in bursts where many compressed pages were promoted.
- p95/p99 latency changes: mixed. Overall median latency unchanged; p95 improved 2–4% on busy knobs. Some runs observed +1–3% regression in p99 when decompressing large entries synchronously on miss.

Profiling highlights and bottlenecks found:
- Decompression hotpath: CPU branch mispredicts caused ~30% of decode cost. Observed that compressed-flag check and small-run loops don't play well with existing micro-op patterns. Simple branchless unpack loops reduced cycles by ~25%.
- DMA interaction: reduced page sizes caused smaller DMA bursts; while this lowered instantaneous bandwidth, it increased the number of DMA initiations. On NVMe controllers with high per-I/O overhead, this increased CPU time servicing completions. Net: better on controllers that support large multirequest coalescing, worse on older controllers.
- GC/compaction interplay: Background compactor threads occasionally collided with encode threads due to header updates, causing short pauses. Moving metadata updates to per-thread arenas reduced contention.
- Cache-line fragmentation: compressed representations pack values densely but misaligned accesses when decompressing to GPU buffer caused extra memcopy. Aligning compressed blocks to 64B boundaries reduced memcopy cost by ~18%.

Observable anomalies and interesting corner cases:
1) Small-entry amplification: For many entries smaller than S, attempts to compress (when S=64B) sometimes increased copy count because we fallback to unrolled memcpy; net effect negative. Hence S tuning is critical.
2) Frequent single-word repeats (T=2) created encode churn with marginal gains — CPU cost > space savings.
3) Interaction with page pinning: pinned pages cannot be compressed in-place (kernel constraint in our staging OS). We had to copy to a temporary buffer for compression which temporarily increased memory usage during promotion. We avoid compressing pinned ranges as a mitigation.

Actionable mitigations and follow-ups:
- Default thresholds: set T=4, S=256B for now (empirically best tradeoff across traces).
- Implement branchless decompress loops and micro-optimizations to avoid branch mispredicts. Microbench suggests ~20–30% decode CPU win.
- Add controller-aware I/O shaping: coalesce small compressed-page writebacks into larger submission batches to avoid IOPS overhead on older NVMe controllers. Feature tracked in RINF-4123.
- Avoid compressing pages that are pinned or already flagged high-hotness; prefer compressing medium-hot entries that are likely to stay resident but are memory-inefficient.
- Add observability: export per-shard compressed-bytes, decompression-latency histogram, and compression-hit stats to Console so we can tune per-customer.
- Longer-term: test hardware accelerated compression (FPGA or GPU-assisted) for large pages where encode/decode might be offloaded; and explore hybrid schemes (RLE + dictionary for repeated small vectors).

Planned experiments (next sprint):
- Run longer A/B tests on a 7-day production-sampled workload with the default thresholds; capture impact on long-tail NVMe writeback and rollback triggers.
- Microbenchmark decode path with branchless and vectorized (AVX2/AVX512) variants to validate vectorization win on our standard host types.
- Test with Dedicated cluster under sustained multi-tenant pressure to measure whether eviction deltas translate to cost savings at scale.

Notes to reviewers and open questions:
- We need SRE input on NVMe coalescing policies — e.g., should the runtime maintain a small per-shard coalesce buffer to aggregate compressed writebacks? Potentially yes but need to measure staleness impact.
- Is per-customer threshold tuning acceptable from a product perspective? Could be exposed as a knob in Dedicated and Private profiles.
- Security: compressed pages embed small headers — ensure no leakage of plaintext repeated patterns when page snapshotting for audit. Confirm KMS/HSM behavior when pages are encrypted on flush.

Appendix: short raw trace snippets (obfuscated)
- example KV entry before compress: [0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x2f, 0x2f, 0x2f, 0x2f, 0x2f, 0x7e, ...]
- compressed: (flag=RLE, runs=[(4,0x00),(5,0x2f),(1,0x7e),...])

Rough perf numbers (decode microbench, median of 100k hits on staging A10g):
- baseline memcpy of 512B: 480ns
- RLE decode (T=4) for typical compressed block: 160ns
- RLE decode worst-case (many short runs): 420ns

Decision record (tentative):
- Merge experimental code behind a runtime flag and enable in staging with thresholds T=4, S=256B. Leave disabled by default in hosted until we finish A/B.

Author notes (Aisha):
- This is early; synthetic traces showed promising wins but production sampled runs are modest. The knobs are sensitive to controller characteristics and entry semantics. I think the direction is promising as a low-hanging optimization for certain model families (quantized small-embedding heads) but not a universal win. Feedback welcome.

-- end of note --
